Judicial Review. The power of courts, particularly the Supreme Court of the United States, to examine laws and government actions and determine whether they conform to the Constitution; laws or acts deemed unconstitutional can be struck down and rendered unenforceable. Though not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, the doctrine was first asserted by the Supreme Court in Marbury v. Madison in 1803 and has since become a cornerstone of American constitutional governance. Judicial review enables the judiciary to enforce constitutional limits on legislative and executive power, making it essential to the system of checks and balances.

The Supreme Court first claimed the power of judicial review in Marbury v. Madison when Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Court had authority to void unconstitutional acts of Congress. Judicial review applies to federal laws, state laws, and executive actions; all are subject to scrutiny against constitutional requirements, though the Court exercises this power selectively through its docket discretion. The doctrine rests on the principle that the Constitution is the supreme law of the land; any statute contradicting it is therefore void, and it is the Court's role to say what the Constitution means. Judicial review does not give courts unlimited power; the Court may defer to legislative or executive judgments when constitutional meaning is ambiguous, or when the Constitution grants discretion to the political branches. The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, became a major vehicle for judicial review; the Court has used it to strike down state laws restricting civil rights, particularly after the mid-twentieth-century expansion of constitutional protections. Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 exemplified judicial review's power; the Supreme Court used it to overturn longstanding precedent and declare racial segregation in schools unconstitutional, forcing social change through judicial mandate. Different constitutional eras have seen different levels of judicial activism; the Court in the early twentieth century struck down Progressive legislation, while the mid-twentieth-century Court expanded rights protections. John Marshall, the Chief Justice who first asserted this power, fundamentally shaped American constitutional law through his interpretation of the Court's proper role in the federal system.
